passages.title: The Urban Heat Island Effect
passages.text:
Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, keeping temperatures high after sunset. Buildings also block wind, which would otherwise carry heat away, and the loss of trees removes shade and the cooling that comes from the evaporation of water from leaves. Waste heat from vehicles and air conditioners adds to the problem.

Planners have tested several responses. Light-coloured "cool roofs" reflect more sunlight, and planting trees along streets provides both shade and moisture. Some cities have also introduced green corridors that channel breezes into dense neighbourhoods. Although these measures can lower local temperatures by a few degrees, they require long-term maintenance and often compete with other uses of limited urban land.

Researchers emphasise that the effect is not only a comfort issue. During heat waves, elevated nighttime temperatures prevent the body from recovering, which raises health risks, especially for elderly residents.

passages.title: Campus Tour (Section 2 style)
passages.text:
Welcome to Northfield College. I'll start with the library, which is open from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays but closes at 6 p.m. on Saturdays and stays closed on Sundays. Most students don't realise there's a quiet floor on level three where phones are not allowed. The study rooms on level two can be booked online, up to two hours at a time.

Next, the cafeteria, which was renovated last year and now offers vegetarian meals every day. The most popular dish is the lentil curry. If you prefer something quicker, there's a coffee cart outside the science building.

Finally, the sports hall. It's free for students, but you must register at the front desk with your student card. The swimming pool is currently closed for repairs and should reopen in October.

passages.title: Project Discussion (Section 3 style)
passages.text:
Tutor: So, how is your project on reducing plastic waste on campus going?
Mia: We've surveyed about two hundred students.
Kai: Yes, and the biggest surprise was that most people already carry reusable bottles.
Mia: But they say there are too few refill stations. I think that should be our main recommendation.
Kai: I agree, although I'd also like to include a deposit system for takeaway cups.
Mia: I'm not convinced. It might be too costly to run.
Tutor: Fair point. What about the structure of the report?
Kai: I'd put the survey results first.
Mia: Me too, then recommendations, and costs at the end.
Tutor: And the deadline?
Kai: We hoped for next Friday, but the library data only arrives on Monday.
Tutor: Then I'll give you until the following Wednesday, but no later.

passages.title: Rooftop Gardens in Dense Cities
passages.text:
A. As cities grow denser, the land available for growing food shrinks. Some planners have turned to rooftops, which make up a large share of the unused surface in urban areas. A rooftop garden can supply vegetables to nearby restaurants and households, reducing the distance food must travel.

B. Rooftop gardens also affect the buildings beneath them. A layer of soil and plants insulates the roof, which can lower summer cooling costs and extend the life of the waterproof membrane. However, soil is heavy, and many older buildings cannot support the load without structural reinforcement, an expense that discourages owners.

C. Water management is another benefit. During storms, the soil absorbs a portion of the rainfall that would otherwise rush into drains. Studies of one pilot district found that such roofs held back roughly a third of the water in moderate storms, though the figure fell sharply once the soil was saturated.

D. Critics point out that rooftop produce is rarely cheap. Labour, irrigation and the cost of lifting materials raise prices, and yields per square metre are often lower than on conventional farms. Supporters respond that the real value lies not in competing on price but in freshness, community involvement and education. Several schools use rooftop plots to teach students about nutrition.

E. Looking ahead, some cities offer tax reductions to owners who install green roofs, while others require them on new large buildings. Whether such rules succeed will depend on whether the gardens remain well maintained after the initial enthusiasm fades.

passages.title: Sleep and the Memory Puzzle
passages.text:
A. Researchers have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory, but only in recent decades have experiments begun to show how. In a typical study, volunteers learn a list of word pairs in the evening. Half then sleep normally, while the other half stay awake through the night. When both groups are tested after a recovery period, the sleepers usually recall more pairs.

B. One explanation focuses on the brain's deep-sleep phase, during which recently formed memories appear to be replayed and strengthened. Recordings from animals show that patterns of brain activity seen during learning reappear during later sleep, often at a faster speed.

C. Yet not every kind of memory benefits equally. Skills such as typing sequences seem to improve after sleep, whereas memory for emotionally neutral facts shows smaller gains. Some researchers suspect that the brain gives priority to information it judges likely to be useful.

D. The findings have practical implications. Students who cut sleep to cram before exams may be undermining their own efforts. Some schools have responded by starting lessons later in the morning, although results so far are mixed, and it is difficult to separate the effect of extra sleep from other changes.

E. Despite progress, many questions remain. It is unclear how much sleep is needed for these benefits, and whether short naps can offer the same advantage. Further studies with larger and more diverse groups will be needed.

passages.title: Harbour Point Business Park: Notice to Tenants
passages.text:
From 1 March, the visitor car park will be closed for resurfacing, which is expected to take six weeks. During this period, visitors may use the temporary car park on Dock Road, which is a five-minute walk from the main entrance. A free shuttle will run between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., every fifteen minutes.

Tenants with a permit can continue to use the staff car park but must display their permits clearly. Vehicles without permits may be removed at the owner's expense. The bicycle racks near Building C will remain open.

Tenants who wish to arrange deliveries should notify reception at least one day in advance, as delivery vans cannot enter the main yard during the resurfacing. For questions, contact the facilities office on extension 204 or email facilities@harbourpoint.example.
